info.title: parsec platform tools
info.description: The four RHDP platform tools as parsec implements them, derived from vendor/parsec at 28e2c40. They are one service, not four, because they identify the same things by the same strings and a seed store that disagreed with itself would be unusable: a provision GUID names an AAP2 job (query_aap2), the AnarchySubject and ResourceClaim that launched it (query_babylon_catalog), the sandbox-{guid}-{catalog-item} namespace whose VMs and PVCs it provisioned (query_ocpv_cluster), and the log lines all three wrote (query_splunk). A real investigation walks that chain in one direction or the other -- GUID to job, job to component, component to cluster state, and any of them to Splunk -- so splitting the four into separate services would put the join keys in separate stores and make a consistent seed impossible to express. query_splunk in particular owns no entities of its own; every identifier it takes belongs to one of the other three. Request parameters come from each tool's input_schema in src/agent/tool_definitions.py, cross-checked against the implementation signature, which is where the recorded defaults come from. Response shapes come from the dict each tool's function actually assembles; where a tool dispatches to per-action helpers with different field sets, each helper's shape is its own schema rather than one schema with everything optional. Controller FQDNs are deliberately absent throughout: query_aap2's four short controller names are grounded in vendor/parsec/config/prompts/aap2_agent.md:69-72, but the hostnames -- which is what query_splunk's `controller` parameter and SplunkAap2LogEntry.controller actually carry -- exist for this repo only in a gitignored trace export that holds real production identifiers, and this file is tracked. vendor/parsec/config/prompts/aap2_agent.md:481-485 documents a different query_aap2 response shape (name, elapsed, job_template, and find_jobs returning count) -- that section is stale and the code is authoritative.

tool_registry.x-note: One entry per tool rather than one span covering all four: the four registry entries are not contiguous -- query_icinga sits between query_ocpv_cluster and query_aap2, and this spec does not model it.

Job.description: One AAP2 job as get_job returns it. The state store's `jobs` collection.

log.description: Trimmed stdout of the job, as get_job_log returns it. Absent on a job whose log was not fetched.

log_original_size.description: Byte size of the untrimmed log.

log_trimmed_size.description: Byte size of the log after trimming.

id.description: Storage identity for the `jobs` collection. Synthetic: the simulation store keys rows by it.

job_id.description: AAP2 job id, an integer (src/tools/aap2.py:91). Not the storage key: the jobs collection is keyed by the synthetic `id`.

job_name.description: Encodes catalog item and GUID, e.g. 'RHPDS agd-v2.sovereign-cloud.dev-gm5ld-2-provision-...'.

status.description: Job status. All five values are real; a seed may use any of them.

started.description: Defaults to '' for a job that has not started; not a valid date-time in that case.

finished.description: Defaults to '' for a job that has not finished; not a valid date-time in that case.

duration_seconds.description: Elapsed seconds, integer-truncated. Null when the job has not finished.

job_explanation.description: AAP's own explanation when the job did not run to completion. Often empty.

action.description: From extra_vars ACTION, e.g. provision, destroy, stop, start. 'unknown' when absent.

controller.description: Always the resolved short name, never the hostname the caller passed.

JobWithLog.description: What get_job_log returns: a Job plus its trimmed stdout.

log.description: Trimmed Ansible log. When trimming applied, it opens with the header '[Trimmed Ansible log: N → M lines, ...]'.

log_original_size.description: Length of the raw log in characters.

JobSummary.description: The 9-field projection find_jobs returns. Deliberately fewer fields than Job.

started.description: Defaults to '' for a job that has not started; not a valid date-time in that case.

finished.description: Defaults to '' for a job that has not finished; not a valid date-time in that case.

JobEvent.description: One task-level Ansible event. The state store's `job_events` collection.

controller.description: Controller the job ran on. Part of the event's storage identity.

event_key.description: Stable key for this event within its job.

job_event_id.description: Storage identity for the `job_events` collection. Synthetic: the simulation store keys rows by it.

event.description: Runner event type, e.g. runner_on_ok, runner_on_failed, runner_on_unreachable, runner_on_skipped, runner_retry.

role.description: Role FQCN when the task came from a role, else empty.

stdout.description: Task stdout, truncated at 4000 characters for failed events and 500 otherwise.

error_msg.description: The module's error message. Empty unless the task failed.

counter.description: Monotonic event ordering within the job.

total.description: Number of jobs in `jobs`, after max_results is applied.

controller.description: Required for get_job, get_job_log and get_job_events. Optional for find_jobs, which searches every controller when omitted.

job_id.description: Required for get_job, get_job_log and get_job_events.

template_name.description: find_jobs: case-insensitive substring match on the job name.

max_results.description: Clamped to 200 by the tool regardless of what is asked for -- a request for more is legal and returns 200 results, not an error.

SplunkOcpLogEntry.description: One OCP pod-log row as _slim_ocp_results projects it (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:205-221), used by the search_by_guid and search_namespace actions. This is parsec's own eight-field projection of a federated Splunk row, not the row itself: the raw event is JSON in Splunk's `_raw`, which the SPL `| spath` stage explodes into dotted field names (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:42-44, :55), and this projection keeps eight of them. Every key is always present and every one of the eight falls back to the empty string, so an empty value means the dotted key was absent from the row, never that the log line carried an empty value.

splunk_ocp_log_entry_id.description: Storage identity for the `splunk_ocp_log_entries` collection. Synthetic: the simulation store keys rows by it. Declared because `search_by_guid` and `search_namespace` READ this collection (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:67, :78 -- both target the OCP app index), so without an identity it is not an entity, gets no store table, and those two actions have nothing to read at all.

time.description: Splunk's `_time` for the event, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:211). Passed through verbatim as Splunk rendered it, so `format: date-time` is deliberately not claimed.

namespace.description: `kubernetes.namespace_name`, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:212). This is the field the GUID search actually matches on -- search_by_guid does not filter a namespace field at all, it raw-text-matches the GUID anywhere in the event and relies on the GUID appearing inside the namespace name (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:65-67).

level.description: The log record's own `level`, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:216). Deliberately not an enum: the value is whatever the emitting container wrote, and `errors_only` does not constrain it -- that filter is a raw-text match for the words error, fatal or warning anywhere in the event (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:50-51), so an errors_only result set can carry rows whose `level` is empty or says something else entirely.

message.description: The log record's `message`, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:217). Not truncated -- unlike the AAP2 projection's `stdout`.

cluster.description: `openshift.labels.cluster_name`, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:218). This is the field the `cluster_name` request parameter is *meant* to select on, but that filter is also a raw-text match rather than a field comparison (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:47-49), so it can match the same string appearing elsewhere in the event.

SplunkAap2LogEntry.description: One AAP2 controller-log row as _slim_aap2_results projects it (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:224-245), used by the search_aap2_logs action. Five keys are always present and each falls back to the empty string. The rest are conditional, and that is the shape's whole point: the four task keys are added *as a group* only when `event_data.task` is non-empty (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:235-240), and `stdout` only when non-empty (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:241-243). So a row either carries all four task keys or none of them, and the absence of `task` means the record was a plain controller log line rather than an Ansible task event.

splunk_aap2_log_entry_id.description: Storage identity for the `splunk_aap2_log_entries` collection. Synthetic: the simulation store keys rows by it.

controller.description: `cluster_host_id` from the AAP2 log record, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:230). Note this is the controller *host* as AAP2 logged it, not the short controller name query_aap2 uses -- the two tools identify the same controller by different strings, which is why an investigation crossing them has to translate.

level.description: The record's `level`, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:231). Not an enum, for the same reason as the OCP projection's `level`; note this action's errors_only filter matches a different word list -- ERROR, CRITICAL, WARNING or failed (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:93-94).

logger.description: `logger_name`, the Python logger that emitted the line, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:232).

message.description: The record's `message`, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:233).

task.description: `event_data.task` -- the Ansible task name. Present only when non-empty, and its presence is what admits the other three task keys (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:235-237).

role.description: `event_data.role`, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:238). Present whenever `task` is, including when the role itself is empty -- so unlike `task`, an empty value here is a real emission.

task_action.description: `event_data.task_action` -- the Ansible module the task ran -- or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:239).

stdout.description: The record's `stdout`, truncated to its first 2000 characters, present only when non-empty (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:241-243). The truncation is silent -- no marker is appended, unlike query_aap2's log trimmer, which writes a header.

SplunkSearchResult.description: A completed Splunk search (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:195-202). All six keys are always present. Four of them are the search client's own accounting (vendor/parsec/src/connections/splunk.py:198-203) and two are what the tool decided to run, echoed back. Note what this tool does *not* own: no entity in this response is a query_splunk entity. `guid`, `namespace`, `cluster_name` and `controller` all identify records belonging to the other three tools in this service, which is the reason query_splunk is grouped with them rather than given a service of its own -- a seed where a Splunk row's namespace names no babylon deployment, or its controller no platform job, is internally inconsistent even though every individual record validates.

results.description: The rows, newest first: every generated query ends `| sort -_time` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:55, :98), except a search_raw query, whose ordering is the caller's own business. Item shape depends on the action: search_by_guid and search_namespace rows are slimmed to SplunkOcpLogEntry, search_aap2_logs rows to SplunkAap2LogEntry, and search_raw rows are not slimmed at all (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:190-193) -- they are whatever the caller's SPL projected, so no item schema can describe them.

anyOf.description: search_raw only: an unslimmed Splunk row, whose fields are the caller's own SPL projection.

result_count.description: len(results) (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:197). Bounded by max_results after that value is clamped to 500 (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:162), and equal to `total_count` whenever `truncated` is false.

total_count.description: Splunk's own `resultCount` for the finished job -- how many events matched, before the result fetch was capped -- or 0 when the job reported none (vendor/parsec/src/connections/splunk.py:158, :201). 0 is therefore not proof nothing matched.

truncated.description: True exactly when fewer rows were fetched than Splunk said matched (vendor/parsec/src/connections/splunk.py:202). Computed from a comparison, not from a cap being hit, so it stays false when the counts happen to agree at the cap.

query.description: The SPL actually executed, including the `index=` clause, every filter the tool appended, and the trailing `| spath | sort -_time` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:46-55, :89-98). For search_raw it is the caller's own query, stripped of surrounding whitespace and otherwise unmodified (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:105, :112). Every interpolated value has had double quotes, single quotes and backslashes deleted first (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:19-21), so a value containing them appears here without them.

index.description: Which index the action targeted, or the literal `custom` for search_raw, where the index is inside the caller's own query (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:112). The `federated:` prefix is not decoration -- it routes the search to Splunk Cloud through the on-prem REST endpoint (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:11-13). The enum below is the emittable set, which is narrower than what the tool advertises: a third index constant, federated:rh_pds-001_ocp_infra, is defined (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:15) and named in the tool's own description (vendor/parsec/src/agent/tool_definitions.py:981), but no action selects it -- _build_ocp_query hard-codes the app index (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:46), so infra logs are reachable only by writing the index into a search_raw query (vendor/parsec/config/prompts/babylon_agent.md:35-36, :68), which reports `custom` here.

QuerySplunkRequest.description: Parameters from the tool's input_schema (vendor/parsec/src/agent/tool_definitions.py:974-1048), cross-checked against the implementation signature, which is where the recorded defaults come from -- the input_schema declares them in prose only (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:140-151). Every omitted string parameter defaults to the empty string, which is also how each action's own required-parameter check is written: it tests falsiness, so an explicitly empty string is rejected exactly like an absent one.

action.description: Which search to run. Each action requires a different parameter and rejects the request in-band without it: search_by_guid needs `guid`, search_namespace needs `namespace`, search_aap2_logs needs `controller`, search_raw needs `raw_query` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:126-133).

guid.description: Provision GUID. Required for search_by_guid, where it is matched as raw text anywhere in the event because the GUID appears inside OCP namespace names (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:65-67). Optional for search_aap2_logs, where it narrows the controller's log to one provision (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:90-92). Ignored by the other two actions.

namespace.description: Kubernetes namespace. Required for search_namespace. Despite the action's name it is not an exact field match either -- the namespace is interpolated as a quoted raw-text term (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:76-78), so a shorter namespace name that is a substring of a longer one will match both.

cluster_name.description: OCP cluster domain, an optional additional raw-text filter on the two OCP searches (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:47-49). Ignored by search_aap2_logs and search_raw. The tool's own description gives an example FQDN (vendor/parsec/src/agent/tool_definitions.py:1011-1013); no example value is declared here, for the same reason this service's controller FQDNs are absent.

controller.description: AAP2 controller *hostname*, required for search_aap2_logs (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:85-89). Not the short controller name QueryAap2Request.controller takes -- that enum's four values will not match anything here, and the value that does match is what SplunkAap2LogEntry.controller reports. The tool's description gives an example FQDN (vendor/parsec/src/agent/tool_definitions.py:1015-1019); no example value is declared here.

search_terms.description: Additional raw text to require in the event, appended as a quoted term by the three generated queries (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:52-54, :95-97). Ignored by search_raw.

earliest.description: Start of the search window in Splunk's own time syntax, passed through to the search job unvalidated (vendor/parsec/src/connections/splunk.py:132-136). The tool's description gives -7d, -1h and an absolute ISO timestamp as further forms (vendor/parsec/src/agent/tool_definitions.py:1029). Applies to search_raw too, so a raw query is still bounded by this window unless it sets its own.

latest.description: End of the search window, same syntax and same passthrough (vendor/parsec/src/connections/splunk.py:135).

errors_only.description: Adds a raw-text severity filter to the generated queries -- error/fatal/warning for the OCP searches, ERROR/CRITICAL/WARNING/failed for AAP2 (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:50-51, :93-94). It is a text match, not a field comparison, so it neither guarantees nor requires that a returned row's `level` says any of those words. Ignored by search_raw.

raw_query.description: SPL for search_raw. Rejected in-band unless it starts with `search ` or `|` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:105-107), and again if it contains any of six write-side commands -- | delete, | outputlookup, | sendalert, | collect, | outputcsv, | sendemail -- matched case-insensitively as substrings (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:24-31, :108-111). That is a denylist, so it is the read-only guarantee's weakest point; it is stated here as what the code checks, not as a claim that nothing else can write.

max_results.description: How many rows to fetch. Clamped to 500 by the tool before the search runs (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:162), so a request for more is legal and returns at most 500 rows rather than an error. It bounds the fetch, not the search: `total_count` still reports everything that matched.

OcpvPvc.description: One PersistentVolumeClaim as _list_pvcs projects it (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:184-191). Six keys are always present; `events` is added only for a Pending claim, and only when the events lookup both succeeded and found something (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:194-210). Note the three literal fallbacks, because each one is indistinguishable from a real value: an absent phase becomes the string `Unknown`, an absent storageClassName becomes an empty string, and an absent storage request becomes `?`.

cluster.description: OCP-V cluster the object lives on. Storage scope: `list_vms` and `list_pvcs` resolve a cluster and then read this collection within it, so a row without it cannot be found.

namespace.description: Namespace the object lives in. Storage scope: both listing actions read this collection *by namespace*, so a row without it is unreachable.

ocpv_pvc_id.description: Storage identity for the `ocpv_pvcs` collection. Synthetic: the simulation store keys rows by it.

name.description: metadata.name, read without a fallback -- a claim with no name would raise, and the outer handler would turn that into the error shape (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:185, :92-94).

status.description: status.phase, or the literal `Unknown` when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:179). Not an enum: the value is whatever Kubernetes reported, plus that fallback. `Pending` is the one value the code itself acts on -- it drives `pending_count` and the `events` lookup.

storage_class.description: spec.storageClassName, or an empty string when the claim does not name one (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:187). An empty value means unset, which in Kubernetes means the cluster default applies -- not that no class was used.

size.description: spec.resources.requests.storage as written, e.g. 100Gi, or the literal `?` when any level of that path is missing (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:188). No unit normalisation is done here, unlike the PV summary's `bound_capacity_gi`.

volume_mode.description: spec.volumeMode, or the literal `Filesystem` when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:189). That fallback restates Kubernetes' own default, so it is usually right -- but it is still a value the tool wrote, not one the API returned. Not an enumeration: Kubernetes accepts both `Filesystem` and `Block` for spec.volumeMode, and parsec copies whichever the PVC declares. The `default` above is parsec's fallback for an absent value, not the only legal value, so a stored row may hold `Block`.

access_modes.description: spec.accessModes verbatim, or an empty array when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:190). Values are Kubernetes' own, e.g. ReadWriteOnce.

events.description: The last three namespace events for this claim, each formatted `reason: message` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:203-206). Present only for a Pending claim whose event lookup returned at least one event; a lookup that raised is swallowed silently (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:209-210), so absence means either no events or a failed lookup, and the two cannot be told apart.

OcpvPvSummaryRow.description: One (node, storage class) group in the cluster-wide PV summary (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:253-260). Not a PV: _list_pvs never returns individual volumes, only these aggregates, so a caller cannot get a PV's name or claim reference from this action at all. Three literal fallbacks live here and each is a value the tool invented rather than read: `unknown` for a PV with no storageClassName, `unassigned` for one with no usable nodeAffinity, and `Unknown` for a missing phase (which then matches none of the three counted phases, so such a PV raises `total_pvs` while contributing to no counter).

node.description: The node this group's volumes are pinned to, taken from the *last* matchExpression value found while walking spec.nodeAffinity.required.nodeSelectorTerms, or the literal `unassigned` when the walk finds none (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:239-249). The loop does not break, so a PV whose affinity names several nodes is attributed to whichever value the walk reached last.

storage_class.description: spec.storageClassName, or the literal `unknown` when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:235). Lowercase, unlike the `Unknown` used for a missing phase -- the two are different fallbacks for different fields and are not interchangeable.

bound.description: How many volumes in this group are phase Bound (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:268-270).

bound_capacity_gi.description: Summed capacity of the Bound volumes in GiB, and the key the whole summary is sorted by, descending (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:262-270, :276). Only a capacity string containing `Gi` contributes: the parse strips `Gi` and takes the integer, silently suppressing a ValueError, so a Ti-, Mi- or unit-less capacity adds 0 (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:262-266). This figure is therefore a lower bound, not a total.

available.description: How many volumes in this group are phase Available (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:271-272). Their capacity is not summed anywhere.

released.description: How many volumes in this group are phase Released (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:273-274).

OcpvStorageClass.description: One StorageClass as _list_storage_classes projects it (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:293-303). Every key is always present; the three string fields fall back to an empty string and `allow_volume_expansion` to false, so a false here can mean either an explicit false or an absent field.

name.description: metadata.name, read without a fallback (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:295).

provisioner.description: The CSI provisioner, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:296).

reclaim_policy.description: reclaimPolicy, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:297). Not an enum -- the value is whatever the object carried, and an empty string is emitted when it carried none, which no Kubernetes enum admits.

binding_mode.description: volumeBindingMode, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:298). Same reasoning as reclaim_policy.

default.description: Whether the annotation storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class is present on the object -- a membership test, so it is true even when the annotation's value is the string "false" (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:300-301).

ocpv_storage_class_id.description: Synthetic storage key; parsec does not return it. The collection name derives from it, and it lets two clusters hold rows of the same name without the store merging them.

cluster.description: OCP-V cluster the object lives on. Storage scope: list_storage_classes resolves a cluster and reads this collection within it, so a row without it cannot be found.

OcpvVmVolume.description: One entry from a VirtualMachine's template volume list, typed by which volume-source key it carries (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:308-324). `source` is genuinely conditional, not merely optional: it is set for dataVolume, pvc and containerDisk but never for cloudInit or other, so those two entries have exactly two keys. That is why `required` names only `name` and `type`.

name.description: The volume's name within the VM spec, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:310).

type.description: Which volume source the entry uses. Unlike most enums in this spec this one is a genuine emission guarantee: the five values are literals the function itself assigns, in a chain that ends in an unconditional else (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:311-323), so no other value can appear. Note `pvc` rather than persistentVolumeClaim -- the key tested and the value written differ.

source.description: What the volume resolves to, and it means a different thing per type: the DataVolume's name, the PVC's claimName, or the container image (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:313, :316, :321). Each falls back to an empty string. Absent entirely for type cloudInit and type other.

OcpvVmDisk.description: One entry from a VirtualMachine's template disk list (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:367-373). Both keys are always present and both fall back to an empty string.

name.description: The disk's name, which is what ties it to an OcpvVmVolume of the same name, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:369).

bus.description: The bus from the disk's `disk` block, falling back to its `cdrom` block and then to an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:370). The fallback is a `.get("disk", .get("cdrom", {}))` chain, so a cdrom device reports its bus here with nothing marking it as a cdrom rather than a disk.

OcpvVmCondition.description: The *first* VirtualMachineInstance condition whose status is the string "False" and which carries a message (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:327-336). Attached to a VM only when that VM is not ready and such a condition exists, so it is the tool's one-line answer to "why is this VM not up" -- and it is only the first such condition, never the full list, so a VM failing for several reasons reports one of them.

type.description: The condition's type, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:332). Kubernetes' own vocabulary, not an enum here.

reason.description: The condition's reason, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:333).

message.description: The condition's message, truncated to its first 200 characters with no marker appended (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:334). Read without a fallback, which is safe because a message is what qualified the condition for selection.

OcpvVm.description: One VirtualMachine joined to its VirtualMachineInstance (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:379-397). The join is by name against the VMIs listed separately for the same namespace (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:412-418); a VM with no running VMI still appears, with the VMI-derived fields at their empty values. Two fields are deliberately nullable rather than empty-string: `node` and `ip` are written as `value or None`, which collapses "the VMI reported nothing" and "there is no VMI" into null. `condition` is present only when the VM is not ready and a failing condition was found.

cluster.description: OCP-V cluster the object lives on. Storage scope: `list_vms` and `list_pvcs` resolve a cluster and then read this collection within it, so a row without it cannot be found.

namespace.description: Namespace the object lives in. Storage scope: both listing actions read this collection *by namespace*, so a row without it is unreachable.

ocpv_vm_id.description: Storage identity for the `ocpv_vms` collection. Synthetic: the simulation store keys rows by it.

name.description: metadata.name of the VirtualMachine, read without a fallback (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:341).

status.description: status.printableStatus -- KubeVirt's own summary word, e.g. Running or Stopped -- or the literal `Unknown` when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:343). Not an enum: KubeVirt's set is long and this adds a fallback outside it.

OcpvNamespaceLookup.description: action=find_namespace: which OCPV cluster holds a namespace (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:146-150). This is the discovery action every other namespace-scoped action falls back to when no cluster is given (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:36-44, :84-87), so its answer is what makes the rest of the tool usable from a namespace alone. It returns on the *first* cluster where the namespace GETs successfully, in configured order, and any non-404 error is logged and skipped exactly like a 404 (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:151-156) -- so a cluster that was merely unreachable is reported the same as one that genuinely lacks the namespace. The not-found branch instead carries `error` plus `clusters_searched`; that field is allowlisted in the coverage map rather than declared here, because this schema models the success shape. **Simulation storage.** The `ocpv_namespaces` collection is the sole authority for which cluster holds which namespace: one row per (cluster, namespace) pair, carrying that pair plus the namespace status. There is no separate per-cluster namespace inventory anywhere in this store. `find_namespace` must therefore be answered by looking the requested `namespace` up in `ocpv_namespaces` and returning the matching row's `cluster`, and the not-found branch is only correct when no row matches. Deciding from the set of configured cluster short names instead is wrong and reports a namespace that is present in the store as missing. The same collection is what makes the implicit cluster discovery the other namespace-scoped actions fall back on work.

deployerJob.description: The same deployerJob field, under _extract_anarchy_subject_info's name (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:493).

completeJob.description: The AAP2 job id for the *complete* (destroy) action (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:494). Only _extract_anarchy_subject_info asks for it; _extract_anarchy_state's field map does not, so it never appears on a component's tower_jobs.

BabylonProvisionData.description: The sandbox and cloud identifiers a ResourceClaim's status summary carries (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:322-343). Almost everything here is conditional: only `cloud_provider` and `guid` are unconditional, the three AWS keys appear only when the summary named an aws_sandbox_account_id, and `cnv_cluster` only when cloud_provider is exactly openshift_cnv. So an object with two keys is normal, not truncated. This is the shape that ties a Babylon deployment to a sandbox account in the cloud service and to a GUID the platform service's jobs and the OCPV namespaces also carry.

cloud_provider.description: summary.provision_data.cloud_provider, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:321). Not an enum: it is a passthrough, and the one value the code itself tests for is the literal openshift_cnv (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:338).

guid.description: The provision GUID, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:324). One of the two places list_deployments' `guid` filter looks; the other is instance_vars.guid (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:957-962).

aws_region.description: aws_default_region, falling back to aws_region and then to an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:330). Present only alongside sandbox_account_id.

sandbox_account_id.description: aws_sandbox_account_id -- the 12-digit AWS account, and the key list_deployments' `account_id` filter compares by exact equality (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:331, :953-956). Its presence is what admits the other two AWS keys. Present for CNV items too when they provision anything on AWS (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:326-327).

sandbox_name.description: The first dot-separated label of aws_route53_domain, e.g. the sandbox4440 of sandbox4440.opentlc.com (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:332-336). Present only when that domain was set. Matches the `name` primary key of the cloud service's sandbox account records.

cnv_cluster.description: sandbox_openshift_cluster, falling back to openshift_cluster_ingress_domain and then to an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:339-342). Present only when cloud_provider is openshift_cnv. This is the pointer into query_ocpv_cluster's territory -- but note it is a cluster *domain or URL*, not the ocpv08-style short name that tool's `cluster` parameter takes.

BabylonResourceClaimRef.description: A name/namespace pointer to a ResourceClaim, read from an AnarchySubject's poolboy annotations (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:475-478). Present on a subject only when the claim-name annotation is non-empty; the namespace half is read with an empty-string fallback and is emitted regardless, so an entry with an empty `namespace` is possible.

name.description: The poolboy.gpte.redhat.com/resource-claim-name annotation (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:475). Feed it to get_deployment together with `namespace`.

namespace.description: The poolboy.gpte.redhat.com/resource-claim-namespace annotation, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:476).

BabylonExpectedInstance.description: One instance an AgnosticVComponent definition is expected to create. Six extraction patterns feed this one shape and they disagree about which keys they set (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:148-244), so only `purpose` and `count` are common to all -- and even `instance_type` is absent for a CNV entry, which reports `cores`/`memory` instead. An entry is kept only if it ended up with either an instance_type or a cores value (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:179-180), which is the one guarantee the shape does make. Three fallback literals here are the tool's inventions, not the definition's: an unnamed instance becomes purpose `unknown`, an unnamed machineset group becomes purpose `machineset_machineset`, and a ROSA definition with no compute type declared is reported as m5.xlarge with 2 replicas -- a concrete, plausible-looking answer to a question the definition did not answer.

purpose.description: What the instance is for. From the definition's instance name, falling back to the literal `unknown` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:159); or a role name from a fixed list -- bastion, master, worker, node, control_plane, infra (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:188-194); or the literal `rosa_worker`; or `machineset_<group name>`, where the group name itself falls back to the literal `machineset` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:223, :238-241).

count.description: How many. From the definition's own count with a fallback of 1 (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:160); or resolved from four naming conventions -- <role>_instance_count, num_<role>s, num_<role>, <role>_count -- again falling back to 1 (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:198-209); or a machineset's total_replicas falling back to replicas then 1 (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:237). The role path coerces to int, the others do not, so a definition whose replica count is a string emits a string here.

image.description: The definition's image, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:161). Set by the instances-list pattern only -- never by the role, ROSA or machineset patterns.

instance_type.description: The cloud instance type. Absent for a CNV entry, which sizes by cores and memory instead. From a flavor_<cloud> or flavor map keyed by ec2/aws/azure/gcp (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:163-174), from a <role>_instance_type or <role>_instance_flavor variable that is a string and contains no Jinja (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:190-192), from rosa_compute_machine_type defaulting to m5.xlarge (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:219), or from a machineset group's instance_type.

cloud.description: Which cloud the instance_type belongs to. `ec2` is normalised to `aws`, so the four emittable values are aws, azure, gcp and cnv -- cnv being written when the entry has cores or memory (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:167, :173, :178, :226). Absent for the role and machineset patterns, which never set it. Declared as an enum because each value is a literal the function assigns, not something read from the definition.

cores.description: The definition's cores, present only for a CNV entry, and read with no fallback -- so it is null when the definition has a memory key but no cores (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:175-178).

memory.description: The definition's memory, present only for a CNV entry, read with no fallback and so null when the definition has cores but no memory (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:175-177).

BabylonSubComponent.description: One entry of a multi-component catalog item's composition, from the definition's __meta__.components (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:894-901). Present only when that list exists and is a list. Worth having because a multi-component item is where failures hide: the sandbox half can provision while the lab half fails (vendor/parsec/config/prompts/babylon_agent.md:203-208).

name.description: The component's name within the item, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:896).

item.description: The catalog item the component refers to, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:897). Feed it back to get_component to descend.

BabylonWorkshopAsset.description: One asset of a MultiWorkshop -- a workshop offering within a multi-asset event (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:605-614). Every key is always present and every one falls back to an empty string. Non-dict entries in the spec's assets list are skipped silently (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:603-604), so `asset_count` can be lower than the object actually declares.

name.description: The asset's name, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:607).

key.description: The asset key, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:609).

type.description: The asset type, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:610). Not an enum -- a passthrough of whatever the spec named.

namespace.description: The asset's namespace, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:611).

workshop_id.description: workshopId -- the id tying this asset to a Workshop object -- or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:612).

BabylonAnarchyComponentState.description: State extracted from an AnarchySubject embedded in a ResourceClaim's status.resources (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:388-415). Returned empty -- no keys at all -- when the embedded object's kind is not AnarchySubject (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:393-394), which is why `required` is empty: this shape is merged into a component, and the merge can contribute nothing. `tower_jobs` is added only when at least one towerJobs entry survived extraction.

current_state.description: spec.vars.current_state of the embedded AnarchySubject, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:398). Babylon's own lifecycle vocabulary -- the two values the source itself names are the literal `destroyed`, which list_anarchy_subjects filters out when no GUID was given (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1063-1066), and `provision-error`, the state parsec's playbook treats as a failure (vendor/parsec/config/prompts/babylon_agent.md:208-214). Not an enum: it is a passthrough with an empty-string fallback, and no complete list of states exists in parsec's source.

desired_state.description: spec.vars.desired_state, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:399). Compare against current_state to see whether the component is converged or stuck.

guid.description: spec.vars.job_vars.guid, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:400). The per-component GUID, which is what makes a multi-component claim traceable to several provisions.

tower_jobs.description: AAP2 job references keyed by lifecycle action name -- provision, destroy, start, stop -- as towerJobs named them (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:403-414, :297). Absent when no entry had anything truthy in it. This caller's field map produces the `controller`/`job_id`/`status`/`completed` key names.

BabylonResourceComponent.description: One resource of a ResourceClaim -- in practice one AnarchySubject -- as _extract_resource_components projects it (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:418-451). Composed with allOf because the state half is merged in from _extract_anarchy_state and is a separately anchored shape; the drift checker deliberately does not flatten that. Reading *all* of these rather than only the first is the point of the function, and parsec's playbook is explicit that the failure is often on a secondary component (vendor/parsec/config/prompts/babylon_agent.md:203-208).

name.description: The resource's name within the claim, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:434).

healthy.description: The resource's own healthy flag, read with **no** fallback, so it is null when absent rather than false (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:435). Null and false mean different things: nothing reported versus reported unhealthy.

ready.description: The resource's ready flag, likewise null when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:436).

anarchy_subject.description: The referenced AnarchySubject's name, or an empty string; present only when the resource carries a reference block (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:440-442). Worth counting the characters: a name over 63 characters is itself the root cause of a missing AnarchySubject, because Kubernetes rejects it, and parsec's playbook says to check that before making any further tool call (vendor/parsec/config/prompts/babylon_agent.md:44-52).

anarchy_namespace.description: The reference's namespace, or an empty string; present under the same condition as anarchy_subject (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:443).

BabylonResourceClaimTraversal.description: One ResourceClaim as the workshop traversals fetch it (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1164-1195). Two shapes under one name, and they share only `name`: a claim that could not be fetched yields exactly `{name, error}` and nothing else (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1179-1181), so a caller must check for `resources` before reading it. Note the traversal fetches each claim by name in the *Workshop's* namespace, which is why a claim in another namespace fails here rather than being found.

name.description: The claim's name, taken from the Workshop's status.resourceClaims key rather than from the fetched object (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1166, :1185). So it is present even when the fetch failed.

state.description: status.summary.state, or the literal `unknown` when any level of that path is missing (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1186). Absent on the failed-fetch shape.

healthy.description: status.healthy, read with no fallback and so null when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1187).

resources.description: Every AnarchySubject component of the claim, in status.resources order (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1192). Empty when the claim has no resources; absent on the failed-fetch shape.

BabylonPodLogEntry.description: One Babylon management pod's logs (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1660-1669). The same six keys as the OCPV pod-log entry, produced by near-identical code, with one difference in the secret handling: here a line matching the secret pattern is dropped (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1656-1657), the same as OCPV, but the pattern is babylon's own shorter key-name list rather than ocpv's (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:64-68). Dropping is silent either way, so a gap in the log is invisible.

pod.description: The pod's name, read without a fallback (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1628).

phase.description: status.phase, or the literal `Unknown` when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1629).

containers.description: The names of the pod's spec containers (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1630).

log_lines.description: How many lines survived grep, the max_results cut and secret stripping (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1665).

logs.description: The surviving lines joined by newlines, or the literal `(no matching lines)` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1666). A failed log fetch puts the single line `[Error fetching logs: ...]` here as content rather than returning an error (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1643-1644).

grep.description: The term applied, or the literal `(none)` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1667). Note the term is `search` falling back to `guid` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1648), so passing both silently ignores the GUID -- the OCPV twin has no such fallback because it takes no guid.

BabylonProvisionCount.description: A Workshop's or MultiWorkshop's provision tally (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:531-541). All four keys are always present and each falls back to 0, including when status.provisionCount is absent or not a dict, so an all-zero tally does not distinguish a workshop nobody has ordered from one whose status has not been written.

active.description: provisionCount.active, or 0 (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:538). Summed across child workshops into a MultiWorkshop's summary.

failed.description: provisionCount.failed, or 0 (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:539). The number an event-failure investigation is looking for; also summed into a MultiWorkshop's summary.

BabylonCatalogItem.description: One CatalogItem as search_catalog projects it (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:121-145). `ci_name` is the interesting field: the CRD name has its stage suffix split off when the last dot-separated part is one of prod, dev, event or test, and that stripped suffix also becomes `stage` when the stage label was empty (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:129-135). A name ending in anything else keeps its full name as ci_name. parsec's own prompt documents a four-field version of this shape (vendor/parsec/config/prompts/babylon_agent.md:253-254); that is a subset rather than a contradiction, and the code is authoritative.

ci_name.description: The catalog item name with a recognised stage suffix removed (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:132, :135). This is what the `search` filter matches against, along with display_name and keywords, and what the `env_type` filter substring-matches (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:809-814).

namespace.description: metadata.namespace, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:140). In practice one of the three catalog namespaces the action lists from -- babylon-catalog-prod, babylon-catalog-event, babylon-catalog-dev (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:31). Not an enum, because the fallback is outside that set.

stage.description: The babylon.gpte.redhat.com/stage label, or -- when that label is empty and the name ended in a recognised suffix -- that suffix, one of prod, dev, event or test (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:130-133). Not an enum: the label's value is a passthrough and is not restricted to those four.

multiuser.description: spec.multiuser, or false when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:142). A multiuser item is what a Workshop provisions.

asset_uuid.description: The gpte.redhat.com/asset-uuid label, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:143).

keywords.description: spec.keywords, or an empty array (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:144). Joined into the searchable text, so a `search` term can match on a keyword alone.

babylon_catalog_item_id.description: Synthetic storage key; parsec does not return it. The collection name derives from it, and it lets two clusters hold rows of the same name without the store merging them.

cluster.description: Babylon cluster the ResourceClaim lives on. Storage scope: search_catalog resolve a cluster and read this collection within it, so a row without it cannot be found.

BabylonProvisionSummary.description: The provisioning half of a ResourceClaim, from its status.summary (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:310-344). Never a response on its own: it is merged into a deployment with dict.update, and only when status.summary is non-empty (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:367-369), which is exactly why `required` here is empty -- a deployment with no summary carries none of these keys, and requiring any of them would make a legitimate response invalid.

state.description: summary.state, or the literal `unknown` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:313). Note the merge *overwrites* the deployment's own `state`, which was initialised to the same literal (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:363), so `unknown` can arrive by either route and the two are indistinguishable.

agnosticv.description: summary.agnosticv verbatim, or an empty object (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:314). Passed through with no field assignment of parsec's own, so no structure is claimed for it here.

runtime_default.description: summary.runtime_default, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:315). A duration as the summary wrote it; no parsing is done.

provision_data.description: Present only when summary.provision_data is non-empty -- the function returns early without it otherwise (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:318-320, :343).

BabylonDeployment.description: One ResourceClaim as list_deployments and get_deployment project it (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:347-385). Composed with allOf: the summary half is merged in from _extract_provision_data, a separately anchored shape, and the drift checker deliberately does not flatten that. Three keys below are conditional together -- current_state, desired_state and instance_vars are set only when the claim's first resource embeds an AnarchySubject (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:372-383) -- and note that only the *first* resource is read here, unlike the workshop traversals, which read all of them. So a multi-component claim's secondary failures are invisible in this shape.

name.description: metadata.name, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:355). What the `search` filter matches first, and what get_deployment takes as `name`.

namespace.description: metadata.namespace, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:356).

catalog_item.description: The babylon.gpte.redhat.com/catalogItemName label, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:357). The `search` filter's second target.

catalog_namespace.description: The babylon.gpte.redhat.com/catalogItemNamespace label, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:358).

asset_uuid.description: The gpte.redhat.com/asset-uuid label, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:359).

lifespan.description: spec.lifespan verbatim, or an empty object (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:360). A passthrough of poolboy's own shape; parsec assigns no field of it, so none is declared.

healthy.description: status.healthy, read with **no** fallback and so null when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:361).

state.description: Initialised to the literal `unknown` and then overwritten by the summary merge when there is a summary (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:363, :367-369). Always present, therefore, and `unknown` means either no summary or a summary that said `unknown`.

current_state.description: The first resource's embedded AnarchySubject spec.vars.current_state, or an empty string; the key is absent altogether when that resource is not an AnarchySubject (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:375-377).

desired_state.description: The same vars' desired_state, under the same condition (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:378).

instance_vars.description: The AnarchySubject's job_vars, filtered to deployment-relevant keys and stripped of secrets (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:380-383). The filter is a keyword allowlist -- twenty substrings including guid, instance, region, sandbox, worker (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:248-280) -- so this is a projection of job_vars, not job_vars. Any key whose name matches a secret pattern or is in the exact secret-key set is dropped, not masked (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:71-94, :276-277). `guid` is the key list_deployments' guid filter falls back to.

babylon_deployment_id.description: Synthetic storage key; parsec does not return it. The collection name derives from it, and it lets two clusters hold rows of the same name without the store merging them.

cluster.description: Babylon cluster the ResourceClaim lives on. Storage scope: list_deployments and get_deployment resolve a cluster and read this collection within it, so a row without it cannot be found.

BabylonAnarchySubject.description: One AnarchySubject as list_anarchy_subjects projects it (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:454-500). An AnarchySubject is an active provision, so this is the shape a GUID search lands on, and its `tower_jobs` is the hop to the platform service's job records. Three keys are conditional: `resource_claim` needs the poolboy claim-name annotation, `requester_email` needs the requester annotation to be non-empty, and `tower_jobs` needs at least one usable towerJobs entry. parsec's prompt documents a five-field version of this shape (vendor/parsec/config/prompts/babylon_agent.md:256-257) -- a subset, not a contradiction.

cluster.description: Babylon cluster this subject lives on. **Simulation storage scope:** `list_anarchy_subjects` and `list_anarchy_actions` resolve a cluster (explicit `cluster`, else each configured cluster in order) and then read this collection *within it*, so a row without `cluster` is unreachable and the action returns an empty list. parsec itself does not return this field -- the cluster is the request parameter, echoed at the top of the response -- but the store needs it to know which cluster a row belongs to. A 2026-09-14 freeze made this visible: the same seeded subject that a pre-v0.2.0 bundle returned came back as `subjects: []`, because that bundle silently ignored the cluster filter.

babylon_anarchy_subject_id.description: Storage identity for the `babylon_anarchy_subjects` collection. Synthetic: the simulation store keys rows by it.

name.description: metadata.name, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:466). The `search` filter's first target, and the fallback the `guid` filter uses -- a subject matches on guid if either instance_vars.guid equals it or the *name contains* it (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1056-1059).

namespace.description: metadata.namespace, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:467). Meaningful because the default listing is cluster-wide across all babylon-anarchy-* namespaces.

governor.description: spec.governor -- the AnarchyGovernor driving this subject's lifecycle -- or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:468). The `search` filter's second target.

current_state.description: spec.vars.current_state, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:469). Load-bearing for the listing itself: with no `guid` given, a subject whose current_state is exactly the literal `destroyed` is dropped from the result to reduce noise, while a GUID search returns every state including destroy failures (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1061-1066). So an unfiltered listing is not a complete listing.

healthy.description: spec.vars.healthy, read with **no** fallback and so null when absent (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:471). Note it comes from the subject's own vars, not from a status block.

resource_claim.description: Present only when the poolboy resource-claim-name annotation is non-empty (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:475-478). **Simulation storage: keep this INLINE on the subject row as an object with `name` and `namespace`.** It is a name/namespace pointer, not an entity: it has no identity of its own, no collection anywhere in this store, and nothing ever looks a ResourceClaim up on its own. A 2026-09-14 freeze flattened it to a bare reference string, which both drops the namespace half and makes a correctly seeded subject row fail validation. Declared inline rather than as a $ref for exactly that reason.

name.description: The poolboy.gpte.redhat.com/resource-claim-name annotation (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:476).

namespace.description: The poolboy.gpte.redhat.com/resource-claim-namespace annotation, read with an empty-string fallback and emitted regardless, so an empty value is possible (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:477).

requester_email.description: The poolboy.gpte.redhat.com/resource-requester-email annotation, present only when non-empty (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:479-481).

instance_vars.description: spec.vars.job_vars run through the same keyword allowlist and secret stripping as a deployment's (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:461, :483-484). Always present, though it can be empty.

tower_jobs.description: AAP2 job references keyed by lifecycle action name (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:488-498). Absent when nothing usable was found. This caller's field map is the one producing `towerHost`/`deployerJob`/`completeJob` names -- *not* the controller/job_id/status/completed names a component's tower_jobs uses.

BabylonResourcePool.description: One poolboy ResourcePool (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:503-528). Pools hold pre-provisioned resources, so this is where a "nothing available" provision failure shows up. `provider_name` and `resource_name` are conditional: both come from the *first* entry of spec.resources, and neither appears when that list is empty or malformed (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:518-526) -- and `provider_name` additionally needs that entry's provider to be a dict.

name.description: metadata.name, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:510). The only field the `search` filter looks at.

namespace.description: metadata.namespace, or an empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:511). In practice always the poolboy namespace, since that is the only one the action lists (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:53, :1094).

Note this is the full configured list rather than the ones actually reached: the loop returns early on the first hit, so a miss means all of them were tried, but a cluster that raised is recorded in `errors` and still appears here.

Three require `name`: get_component, get_workshop and get_multiworkshop (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:830, :1208, :1434). For get_deployment it is the ResourceClaim name, required together with `namespace`. get_babylon_pod_logs uses it as a case-insensitive pod-name substring filter instead (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1619-1621).

Optional but meaningful for three more: it narrows list_anarchy_subjects and list_anarchy_actions from a cluster-wide listing to one namespace, and it lets get_workshop and get_multiworkshop skip their cluster-wide name search. Ignored by search_catalog, which always reads all three catalog namespaces, and by list_resource_pools, which always reads poolboy.

The comment carries the Babylon console URL and the tool matches its domain against the configured clusters' server URLs (vendor/parsec/config/config.yaml:73-76). parsec's guidance is to fetch it from query_aws_account_db first (vendor/parsec/config/prompts/babylon_agent.md:149-150) -- a tool in the cloud service, so this is a documented cross-service join and the value's shape is owned there.

Despite the name it does not compare against any env_type field: a catalog item's env_type lives in its AgnosticVComponent definition, which this action does not fetch. Every other action ignores it.

The three get_* traversals and get_component ignore it entirely, so a MultiWorkshop hierarchy is returned whole however large it is. Not clamped on entry, unlike query_aap2's and query_splunk's -- but it is clamped inside get_babylon_pod_logs, whose per-pod tailLines request is min(max_results, 500) (vendor/parsec/src/tools/babylon.py:1633).

post.summary: Query an AAP2 controller for job metadata, logs, events, or a job search
post.description:
Four actions over the same store.

- `get_job` — one Job by `job_id` on `controller`. Returns all 19 metadata fields.
- `get_job_log` — the same Job plus `log`, `log_original_size`, `log_trimmed_size`. This is the action a real investigation uses (72 of 122 observed calls); prefer it over `get_job`.
- `get_job_events` — that job's task-level events, ordered by `counter` ascending, honouring `failed_only` and `changed_only`. `event_count` always equals the length of `events`. Echo the filters back exactly as received.
- `find_jobs` — search. Returns `{total, jobs}` where each entry is a **JobSummary**: only the nine projection fields, never the full Job. Order by `finished` descending. `total` equals the length of `jobs` after `max_results` is applied, so it is a page count, not a corpus count.

Missing `job_id` or `controller` on a job-specific action, an unknown action, and an unknown controller are all returned in-band as the error shape below. Every failure path the implementation defines returns that shape in-band rather than raising, and for this operation there is one caveat: the max_results clamp runs outside any try block (vendor/parsec/src/tools/aap2.py:462, where the try opens at :464), so a max_results that cannot be compared to an integer would raise out of the tool. That is the identical construct query_splunk caveats. SIMULATION STORE AUTHORITY (this paragraph describes the store, not parsec): `get_job` and `get_job_log` read the `jobs` row whose `job_id` and `controller` match; `find_jobs` reads `jobs` filtered by `controller` and the other supplied filters; `get_job_events` reads the `job_events` rows whose `job_id` and `controller` match. RESPONSE KEYS (parsec's, verbatim, src/tools/aap2.py): get_job returns the stored `jobs` row's metadata fields -- `job_id`, `job_name`, `status`, `failed`, `started`, `finished`, `duration_seconds`, `launch_type`, `job_explanation`, `template_name`, `env_type`, `guid`, `action`, `cloud_provider`, `display_name`, `controller`, plus `git_url`, `git_branch` and `git_revision` when the row carries them (src/tools/aap2.py:69-113) -- and never the storage key `id` or a log field; get_job_log returns those same fields plus `log`, `log_original_size` and `log_trimmed_size` (src/tools/aap2.py:244-257); get_job_events returns `job_id`, `controller`, `event_count`, `filters` (`{failed_only, changed_only}`) and `events`, each event carrying exactly `event`, `task`, `play`, `role`, `host`, `failed`, `changed`, `stdout`, `error_msg` and `counter` (src/tools/aap2.py:179-215, :294-303) and never the storage fields `job_event_id`, `job_id`, `controller` or `event_key`; find_jobs returns `total` and `jobs` (src/tools/aap2.py:386-389), each job carrying exactly the nine JobSummary fields `job_id`, `job_name`, `status`, `failed`, `started`, `finished`, `duration_seconds`, `template_name` and `controller` (src/tools/aap2.py:219-231) -- never `id`, `display_name`, `guid`, `env_type`, `action`, `cloud_provider`, `launch_type`, `job_explanation`, a git field or a log; the key is `total`, never `count`. Return these key names exactly as listed: never rename a key, never replace a list key with the collection name or a generic `items`/`count`, never drop an envelope key, and never echo a storage-only field into a returned element. Each list element is the stored row projected to exactly the fields listed for that action, whatever an example elsewhere in this document shows. A LOG-LESS JOB: get_job_log on a matching `jobs` row that has no stored `log` returns that row's metadata fields with `log: ""`, `log_original_size: 0` and `log_trimmed_size: 0` -- parsec reads an empty stdout for such a job (src/tools/aap2.py:248-256), so this is the documented derivation for a log-less job, not an added value, and it is never an error. The `job not found` error is only for no `jobs` row matching `job_id` and `controller`. FIND_JOBS FILTERS (src/tools/aap2.py:315-322): `status` is an exact match on stored `status`; `template_name` matches when the stored `job_name` contains it, case-insensitively (parsec sends `name__icontains`); `created_after` and `created_before` compare against the stored `started` timestamp, because the store holds no separate creation time -- a row is kept when `started` is strictly after `created_after` and strictly before `created_before`, each date-only bound read as midnight UTC of that date. Apply every supplied filter to every stored row; never drop a row that satisfies all of them. The installed store is the complete dataset for this operation: an empty collection is a deliberate test condition, not missing data or a misconfigured backend. When no stored row matches the request, return the documented empty result -- an empty list with every count at 0 for a listing or search, or an in-band {"error": ...} not-found for a lookup of one named record. Never generate, derive or synthesise a record, row, file or value that is not in the store, and never fill an empty result with plausible data: a stable hash makes an invented value repeatable, not real. This applies to fields as well as records: a stored row carries every field its schema requires, so never compute a missing field of a stored row from a hash of its key or from a range -- return the row exactly as stored. An optional field the stored row omits is omitted from the response, and an optional field the stored row carries is returned unchanged. Every entity in this API is read only through these four store-authoritative operations, so there is no entity for which a record or field may be produced on demand. Only the documented derivations (a count equal to the length of a returned list, a sum of returned amounts) are computed, and only from returned rows.

post.summary: Search Splunk for OCP pod logs and AAP2 controller logs
post.description:
Four searches over two federated Splunk indexes.

- `search_by_guid` — OCP pod logs for a provision GUID, matched as raw text because the GUID appears inside the namespace name. Rows are slimmed to **SplunkOcpLogEntry**.
- `search_namespace` — the same index and the same slimming, keyed on a namespace string instead.
- `search_aap2_logs` — the AAP2 controller log for one controller hostname, optionally narrowed by GUID. Rows are slimmed to **SplunkAap2LogEntry**.
- `search_raw` — the caller's own SPL, run unslimmed. `index` reports `custom`.

Every generated query is raw-text matching plus a trailing `| spath | sort -_time`, never a field comparison: federated search leaves the event as JSON in `_raw`, so the filters run before any field extraction. Two consequences worth honouring in a simulation — a filter can match its string anywhere in the event, and `errors_only` does not constrain a row's `level` field.

This tool owns no entities in the sense that `guid`, `namespace`, `cluster_name` and `controller` all name records belonging to the other three tools in this service -- which is why it is grouped with them: a Splunk row is only meaningful against the platform job, babylon deployment or OCPV namespace it refers to, so the four tools have to agree in one seed store. **It does, however, read a store, and this is where a simulation goes wrong if it is not told so explicitly.** `search_by_guid` and `search_namespace` read the `splunk_ocp_log_entries` collection; `search_aap2_logs` reads `splunk_aap2_log_entries`. Nothing reads both. A filter matches when its string occurs ANYWHERE in a stored row -- that is what raw-text matching means -- and it matches nothing when no stored row contains it. **When no stored row matches, return the normal success shape with an EMPTY `results` list and `result_count` 0. Never synthesise a log entry, and never rewrite a stored row so that it mentions the requested guid, namespace or controller.** An empty result is a real and common answer here: a provision that produced no OCP error events is exactly what the caller needs told, and inventing entries turns a correct 'the logs say nothing' into a fabricated root cause. Measured 2026-09-14, before this paragraph existed: `search_by_guid` for a guid absent from every seeded row returned three invented ERROR entries naming that guid, on a cluster and in a namespace that appear in no seed, and the agent -- correctly, given what it was handed -- reported them as findings.

Every failure path the implementation defines returns the error shape below in-band rather than raising, and for this operation there are two caveats to that sentence. The client lookup is guarded for RuntimeError only (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:154-160), which is sound because that is the only exception it raises (vendor/parsec/src/connections/splunk.py:254-257), but it would not absorb another. And the max_results clamp runs outside any try block (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:162), so a max_results that cannot be compared to an integer would raise out of the tool. Everything from the query build onward is in-band: the per-action validation returns dicts (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:63, :75, :86, :104-111), and the search itself is wrapped in a bare `except Exception` one layer down (vendor/parsec/src/connections/splunk.py:204-207) whose error dict is returned unchanged (vendor/parsec/src/tools/splunk.py:186-187). Return these key names exactly as listed: never rename a key, never replace a list key with the collection name or a generic `items`/`count`, never drop an envelope key, and never echo a storage-only field into a returned element. Each list element is the stored row projected to exactly the fields listed for that action, whatever an example elsewhere in this document shows. post.summary: Inspect an OCPV cluster's storage, VMs, pods, nodes and machines
post.description:
Eleven read-only actions against one OpenShift Virtualization cluster -- the CNV clusters where lab VMs actually run. Six are namespace-scoped (find_namespace, list_pvcs, list_vms, get_ocpv_pod_logs, list_pods, pods_top) and reject the request in-band without `namespace`; the other five are cluster-scoped, which means the *action* ignores `namespace` -- not that the request does. When `cluster` is omitted, `namespace` is the only input to cluster discovery for every action but find_namespace, so calling list_pvs with neither is rejected with 'No cluster specified and could not resolve one' (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:84-87, :44-49).

- `find_namespace` — which cluster holds a namespace. The discovery action the rest depend on: when `cluster` is omitted, every other action calls this first with `namespace`, so a provision GUID is enough to reach the cluster state. Answer it by matching `namespace` in the `ocpv_namespaces` collection and returning that row's `cluster`; never from the list of configured cluster names.
- `list_pvcs` / `list_pvs` / `list_storage_classes` — the storage triple parsec's own playbook walks in that order for a Pending-PVC investigation. `list_pvcs` carries `pending_count` and per-claim events; `list_pvs` returns **aggregates only**, grouped by (node, storage class), never individual volumes.
- `list_vms` — VirtualMachines joined to their VirtualMachineInstances by name, so declared shape and running state appear together, with a failing condition attached to any VM that is not ready.
- `get_node_resources` — declared node capacity. `nodes_top` and `pods_top` are the *usage* actions, read from metrics.k8s.io, with different per-item shapes.
- `get_ocpv_pod_logs` / `list_pods` — pod logs (at most five pods, always) and the cheap phase/restart overview.
- `list_machines` — MachineSets and Machines, two independent listings in one response.

Three things to honour that no schema states. Counts named `count` are page counts, so no field distinguishes a cut list from a complete one. Several fields fall back to invented literals that are indistinguishable from real values -- `Unknown`, `unknown`, `unassigned`, `?`, `(none)`, `(no matching lines)` -- and each one is documented where it occurs. And every capacity figure in GiB is integer-truncated, and the PV sum counts only Gi-suffixed capacities, so those totals are lower bounds.

Every failure path the implementation defines returns the error shape below in-band rather than raising, and for this operation there is no caveat: the whole body from cluster resolution through dispatch sits inside one try block whose handler is a bare `except Exception` (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:76-94). The only statement outside it initialises a local to the empty string (vendor/parsec/src/tools/ocpv.py:75). SIMULATION STORE AUTHORITY (this paragraph describes the store, not parsec): Every action reads its collection filtered first by the stored `cluster` field; a row whose `cluster` differs from the resolved cluster is never a match. `find_namespace` reads `ocpv_namespaces`; `list_vms` reads `ocpv_vms`; `list_pvcs` and `list_pvs` read `ocpv_pvcs`; `list_storage_classes` reads `ocpv_storage_classes`; `list_machines` reads `ocpv_machinesets` and `ocpv_machines` as two separate lists. No collection backs `get_node_resources`, `get_ocpv_pod_logs`, `list_pods`, `nodes_top` or `pods_top`, so those actions always return their documented empty result. post.description:
Twelve read-only actions against the Kubernetes platform that creates, starts, stops and destroys RHDP lab provisions. The largest surface in this service, and the hub of it: a Babylon deployment names the GUID that reaches the OCPV namespace and the Splunk rows, and its components name the AAP2 controller and job id that reach the platform service's own job records.

- `search_catalog` / `get_component` — what an item *should* deploy. search_catalog reads all three babylon-catalog-* namespaces; get_component returns the AgnosticVComponent definition plus derived `expected_instances`, and the agnosticv repo and path to fetch its config from.
- `list_deployments` / `get_deployment` — what *is* deployed: ResourceClaims with sandbox account mappings. Both read only the claim's **first** resource, so a multi-component item's secondary failures are invisible here.
- `list_anarchy_subjects` / `list_anarchy_actions` — active provisions and lifecycle events. Cluster-wide by default; with a `guid` and no `cluster` they search every configured cluster until one matches. A subject's `tower_jobs` is the hop to AAP2.
- `list_resource_pools` — poolboy pool sizing, always in the poolboy namespace.
- `list_workshops` / `get_workshop` / `list_multiworkshops` / `get_multiworkshop` — the workshop family. The two `get_*` actions are deep traversals that fetch every ResourceClaim and extract every AnarchySubject component with its job references; the two `list_*` actions return counts instead. Call list_multiworkshops alongside list_workshops, not instead of it.
- `get_babylon_pod_logs` — pods on the management clusters (poolboy, babylon-anarchy-*), which is where a failure that never reached AAP2 leaves its only trace.
